title: Probability Rules
description: Addition and multiplication rules, disjoint vs independent, conditional and total probability, Bayes, counting, expected value, variance of sums.

cards.title: $P(A) = 0.5$, $P(B) = 0.4$ and $P(A \cap B) = 0.2$. What is $P(A \cup B)$?
cards.body:
0.7

**General addition rule**: $P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B) = 0.5 + 0.4 - 0.2 = 0.7$.

Why: subtract the overlap so it isn't counted twice.
Watch out: only for disjoint events is $P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B)$.
cards.searchQuery: general addition rule P(A or B)

cards.title: Can two disjoint (mutually exclusive) events, each with positive probability, be independent?
cards.body:
No: disjoint events with nonzero probabilities are always **dependent**.

Disjoint means $P(A \cap B) = 0$, but independence would need $P(A \cap B) = P(A)\,P(B) > 0$.

Why: if $A$ happens you know $B$ didn't, so $P(B \mid A) = 0 \ne P(B)$.
cards.searchQuery: disjoint events cannot be independent

cards.title: How do you check whether two events $A$ and $B$ are independent?
cards.body:
Check whether $P(A \cap B) = P(A)\,P(B)$, or equivalently (when $P(B) > 0$) whether $P(A \mid B) = P(A)$.

Example: $P(A) = 0.6$, $P(B) = 0.5$, $P(A \cap B) = 0.3$. Since $0.6 \times 0.5 = 0.3$, $A$ and $B$ are **independent**.
Tip: if the product doesn't match, they're dependent.
cards.searchQuery: how to check independence of two events

cards.title: $P(A \cap B) = 0.12$ and $P(B) = 0.4$. What is $P(A \mid B)$?
cards.body:
0.3

$P(A \mid B) = \dfrac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)} = \dfrac{0.12}{0.4} = 0.3$

Tip: divide by the probability of the condition (the event after the bar).
Watch out: $P(A \mid B)$ and $P(B \mid A)$ are usually different.
cards.searchQuery: conditional probability formula P(A given B)

cards.title: Two cards are drawn without replacement from a standard 52-card deck. What is the probability that both are aces, as a fraction?
cards.body:
$\frac{1}{221} \approx 0.0045$

The draws are dependent, so use the general multiplication rule: $P(A_1 \cap A_2) = P(A_1)\,P(A_2 \mid A_1) = \frac{4}{52} \cdot \frac{3}{51} = \frac{1}{221}$.

Watch out: with replacement (independent draws) it would be $\left(\frac{4}{52}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{169}$.
cards.searchQuery: probability two aces without replacement

cards.title: A fair die is rolled 3 times. What is the probability of at least one 6, as a fraction?
cards.body:
$\frac{91}{216} \approx 0.421$

Use the **complement**: $P(\text{at least one 6}) = 1 - P(\text{no 6s}) = 1 - \left(\frac{5}{6}\right)^3 = 1 - \frac{125}{216} = \frac{91}{216}$.

Watch out: $3 \times \frac{1}{6} = \frac{1}{2}$ overcounts rolls with two or more 6s.
cards.searchQuery: probability at least one six in three rolls complement

cards.title: Machine A makes 60% of a plant's parts (2% defective); Machine B makes 40% (5% defective). What is the probability that a random part is defective?
cards.body:
0.032

$P(D) = P(D \mid A)P(A) + P(D \mid B)P(B) = (0.02)(0.6) + (0.05)(0.4) = 0.012 + 0.020 = 0.032$

Tip: split by source, weight each defect rate by its share, and add.
cards.searchQuery: law of total probability defective parts two machines

cards.title: State Bayes' theorem for $P(A \mid B)$.
cards.body:
$P(A \mid B) = \dfrac{P(B \mid A)\,P(A)}{P(B)}$, where $P(B) = P(B \mid A)P(A) + P(B \mid A^c)P(A^c)$

It reverses a conditional: from $P(B \mid A)$, which you usually know (like a test's accuracy), to $P(A \mid B)$, which you want.

Key idea: the denominator is the law of total probability.
cards.searchQuery: Bayes' theorem formula P(A given B)

cards.title: 1% of people have a disease. A test detects 90% of cases but also flags 5% of healthy people. What is $P(\text{disease} \mid \text{positive})$, to three decimal places?
cards.body:
0.154 (exactly $\frac{2}{13}$)

$P(D \mid +) = \dfrac{(0.90)(0.01)}{(0.90)(0.01) + (0.05)(0.99)} = \dfrac{0.009}{0.0585}$

Watch out: most positives are **false positives**, because healthy people vastly outnumber sick ones (low base rate).
cards.searchQuery: Bayes theorem disease test positive probability

cards.title: When do you count with permutations $P(n, r)$ versus combinations $\binom{n}{r}$, and what are their formulas?
cards.body:
$P(n, r) = \dfrac{n!}{(n - r)!}$ when order matters; $\binom{n}{r} = \dfrac{n!}{r!\,(n - r)!}$ when it doesn't.

Use permutations for rankings and distinct roles, combinations for committees and hands.

Why: $\binom{n}{r} = \dfrac{P(n, r)}{r!}$, since each group of $r$ can be ordered $r!$ ways.
Example: $P(10, 3) = 720$ but $\binom{10}{3} = 120$.
cards.searchQuery: permutations vs combinations formulas order matters

cards.title: How many different 4-person committees can be chosen from 9 people?
cards.body:
126

Order doesn't matter, so use a **combination**: $\binom{9}{4} = \dfrac{9!}{4!\,5!} = \dfrac{9 \cdot 8 \cdot 7 \cdot 6}{4 \cdot 3 \cdot 2 \cdot 1} = \dfrac{3024}{24} = 126$.
cards.searchQuery: combinations committee of 4 from 9 people

cards.title: A game pays 10 dollars with probability 0.2; otherwise you lose 2 dollars. What is the expected value per play, in dollars?
cards.body:
0.40 dollars per play (a 40-cent average gain)

$E(X) = \sum x\,P(x) = 10(0.2) + (-2)(0.8) = 2 - 1.6 = 0.4$

Watch out: it's a long-run average per play. No single play actually pays 40 cents.
cards.searchQuery: expected value of a game payoff

cards.title: $X$ and $Y$ are independent, with $\mathrm{SD}(X) = 3$ and $\mathrm{SD}(Y) = 4$. What is $\mathrm{SD}(X + Y)$?
cards.body:
5

For independent variables, **variances add**, SDs don't: $\mathrm{Var}(X + Y) = 3^2 + 4^2 = 25$, so $\mathrm{SD}(X + Y) = \sqrt{25} = 5$.

Watch out: $3 + 4 = 7$ is the trap.
Tip: means always add: $E(X + Y) = E(X) + E(Y)$.
cards.searchQuery: standard deviation of sum of independent variables

cards.title: For independent $X$ and $Y$, what is $\mathrm{Var}(X - Y)$ in terms of $\mathrm{Var}(X)$ and $\mathrm{Var}(Y)$?
cards.body:
$\mathrm{Var}(X - Y) = \mathrm{Var}(X) + \mathrm{Var}(Y)$, the same as $\mathrm{Var}(X + Y)$.

Subtracting still adds uncertainty: $\mathrm{Var}(X - Y) = \mathrm{Var}(X) + (-1)^2\,\mathrm{Var}(Y)$.

Watch out: the guess $\mathrm{Var}(X) - \mathrm{Var}(Y)$ is wrong and could even be negative.
cards.searchQuery: variance of difference of independent variables

cards.title: In probability, what are the sample space and an event?
cards.body:
The **sample space** $S$ is the set of all possible outcomes of a random process; an **event** is any subset of it.

Example: for two coin flips, $S = \{HH, HT, TH, TT\}$, and the event "exactly one head" is $\{HT, TH\}$.
cards.searchQuery: sample space and event definition probability

cards.title: How many outcomes are in the sample space for flipping a coin 3 times?
cards.body:
8

Each flip has 2 outcomes, so there are $2^3 = 8$ sequences: HHH, HHT, HTH, THH, HTT, THT, TTH, TTT.

Tip: with $n$ flips there are $2^n$.
cards.searchQuery: sample space size flipping coin 3 times

cards.title: What three axioms must every probability assignment satisfy?
cards.body:
Nonnegativity, $P(S) = 1$, and additivity for disjoint events

1. $P(A) \ge 0$ for every event $A$
2. $P(S) = 1$
3. If $A_1, A_2, \dots$ are disjoint, $P(A_1 \cup A_2 \cup \cdots) = P(A_1) + P(A_2) + \cdots$

Key idea: everything else follows, including $P(A) \le 1$ and the complement rule $P(A^c) = 1 - P(A)$.
cards.searchQuery: Kolmogorov axioms of probability

cards.title: When does $P(A) = \dfrac{\text{outcomes in } A}{\text{outcomes in } S}$ give the right probability?
cards.body:
Only when all outcomes in the sample space are **equally likely**.

It works for fair dice, fair coins and well-shuffled cards.

Watch out: it fails for lopsided outcomes. Winning the lottery is not 50% likely just because you either win or lose.
cards.searchQuery: classical probability equally likely outcomes

cards.title: Two fair dice are rolled. What is the probability that the sum is 7, as a fraction?
cards.body:
$\frac{1}{6}$

Of the $6 \times 6 = 36$ equally likely ordered outcomes, six give a sum of 7: $(1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2), (6,1)$. So $P = \frac{6}{36} = \frac{1}{6}$.

Key idea: 7 is the most likely sum.
cards.searchQuery: two dice sum of 7 probability

cards.title: Two fair coins are flipped. What is the probability of two heads, as a fraction?
cards.body:
$\frac{1}{4}$

The equally likely outcomes are HH, HT, TH, TT, and only HH works.

Watch out: answering $\frac{1}{3}$ by treating "0, 1 or 2 heads" as equally likely is wrong. One head can happen in two ways (HT and TH).
cards.searchQuery: two coins probability of two heads

cards.title: A thumbtack lands point-up 312 times in 800 tosses. What is the empirical probability that it lands point-up?
cards.body:
0.39

**Empirical** (relative frequency) probability: $\dfrac{\text{times the event occurred}}{\text{number of trials}} = \dfrac{312}{800} = 0.39$.

Tip: it's an estimate, and it becomes more reliable as the number of trials grows.
cards.searchQuery: empirical probability relative frequency

cards.title: What does the law of large numbers say?
cards.body:
As the number of independent trials grows, the relative frequency of an event gets closer to its true probability (and a sample mean to the population mean).

Watch out: it describes the long run only. It says nothing about the next trial and doesn't make short-run results "even out".
cards.searchQuery: law of large numbers definition

cards.title: A fair coin has landed heads 5 times in a row. What is the probability of heads on the next flip, as a fraction?
cards.body:
$\frac{1}{2}$

Flips are **independent**: the coin has no memory, so tails is never "due". Believing otherwise is the gambler's fallacy.

Why: the law of large numbers works by swamping early streaks with many later flips, not by compensating for them.
cards.searchQuery: gambler's fallacy coin heads in a row

cards.title: An event has probability 0.2. What are the odds in favor of it?
cards.body:
1 to 4 (1:4)

Odds in favor $= \dfrac{p}{1 - p} = \dfrac{0.2}{0.8} = \dfrac{1}{4}$: one success for every four failures, on average.

Watch out: odds of 1:4 are not a probability of $\frac{1}{4}$. The probability is $\frac{1}{1 + 4} = 0.2$.
cards.searchQuery: odds in favor from probability

cards.title: The odds against an event are 7 to 3. What is the probability that it happens?
cards.body:
0.3

Odds against of 7 to 3 mean 7 failures for every 3 successes, so $P = \dfrac{3}{7 + 3} = 0.3$.

Tip: in general, odds in favor of $a$ to $b$ give $P = \dfrac{a}{a + b}$.
cards.searchQuery: probability from odds against

cards.title: In probability notation, what do $A \cup B$, $A \cap B$ and $A^c$ mean?
cards.body:
$A \cup B$: $A$ or $B$ (or both). $A \cap B$: both. $A^c$: not $A$.

The complement is also written $A'$ or $\bar{A}$.

Mnemonic: $\cup$ looks like a cup that holds everything in either set.
cards.searchQuery: union intersection complement notation events

cards.title: $A$ and $B$ are disjoint, with $P(A) = 0.3$ and $P(B) = 0.45$. What is $P(A \cup B)$?
cards.body:
0.75

Disjoint events can't happen together, so $P(A \cap B) = 0$ and the probabilities simply add: $0.3 + 0.45 = 0.75$.

Tip: without disjointness, subtract the overlap (general addition rule).
cards.searchQuery: addition rule for disjoint events

cards.title: $P(A) = 0.6$, $P(B) = 0.3$ and $P(A \cap B) = 0.1$. What is the probability that neither $A$ nor $B$ occurs?
cards.body:
0.2

"Neither" is the complement of "at least one": $P(A \cup B) = 0.6 + 0.3 - 0.1 = 0.8$, so $P(A^c \cap B^c) = 1 - 0.8 = 0.2$.

Why: this uses De Morgan's law, $(A \cup B)^c = A^c \cap B^c$.
cards.searchQuery: probability of neither event De Morgan

cards.title: What are De Morgan's laws for events $A$ and $B$?
cards.body:
$(A \cup B)^c = A^c \cap B^c$ and $(A \cap B)^c = A^c \cup B^c$

In words: "not ($A$ or $B$)" means neither occurs; "not ($A$ and $B$)" means at least one fails.

Tip: to complement, complement each event and swap $\cup$ with $\cap$.
cards.searchQuery: De Morgan's laws for events

cards.title: $P(A) = 0.45$ and $P(A \cap B) = 0.15$. What is the probability that $A$ occurs but $B$ does not?
cards.body:
0.3

$P(A \cap B^c) = P(A) - P(A \cap B) = 0.45 - 0.15 = 0.30$

Tip: remove the overlap from the $A$ circle of the Venn diagram.
cards.searchQuery: probability A occurs but not B Venn diagram

cards.title: $P(A) = 0.5$, $P(B) = 0.3$ and $P(A \cap B) = 0.1$. What is the probability that exactly one of $A$ and $B$ occurs?
cards.body:
0.6

$P(\text{exactly one}) = P(A) + P(B) - 2P(A \cap B) = 0.5 + 0.3 - 0.2 = 0.6$

Why: the overlap is subtracted twice because it is counted in both $P(A)$ and $P(B)$ but belongs to neither "only" region.
cards.searchQuery: probability exactly one of two events occurs

cards.title: $P(A) = 0.6$ and $P(B) = 0.7$. What is the smallest possible value of $P(A \cap B)$?
cards.body:
0.3

Since $P(A \cup B) \le 1$, $P(A \cap B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cup B) \ge 0.6 + 0.7 - 1 = 0.3$.

Key idea: these events can't be disjoint, because their probabilities add to more than 1.
cards.searchQuery: smallest possible P(A and B) given P(A) and P(B)

cards.title: What is the inclusion-exclusion formula for $P(A \cup B \cup C)$?
cards.body:
$P(A) + P(B) + P(C) - P(A \cap B) - P(A \cap C) - P(B \cap C) + P(A \cap B \cap C)$

Adding the three probabilities counts each two-way overlap twice and the triple overlap three times.

Why: subtracting the pairwise terms fixes the doubles but leaves the triple overlap counted zero times, so add it back once.
cards.searchQuery: inclusion-exclusion formula three events

cards.title: An integer is chosen at random from 1 to 100. What is the probability that it is divisible by 2, 3 or 5?
cards.body:
0.74

Inclusion-exclusion on counts: multiples of 2, 3 and 5, minus multiples of 6, 10 and 15, plus multiples of 30: $50 + 33 + 20 - 16 - 10 - 6 + 3 = 74$.

So $P = \frac{74}{100}$.
cards.searchQuery: probability integer 1 to 100 divisible by 2 3 or 5

cards.title: An event has probability $P(A) = 0.35$. What is $P(A^c)$?
cards.body:
$0.65$

**Complement rule**: $P(A^c) = 1 - P(A) = 1 - 0.35 = 0.65$.

Tip: use it whenever "not" is easier to count than the event itself.
cards.searchQuery: complement rule probability of not A

cards.title: Between which two numbers (inclusive) must every probability lie?
cards.body:
0 and 1

Every probability satisfies $0 \le P(A) \le 1$. An impossible event has probability $0$ and a certain event has probability $1$.

Tip: a probability outside this range, such as $1.2$ or $-0.1$, signals a calculation error.
cards.searchQuery: probability must be between 0 and 1

cards.title: In probability, what is a random variable?
cards.body:
A rule that assigns a **number** to each outcome of a random process.

Example: roll two dice. The outcome is a pair like $(3, 5)$, and the random variable $X$ = "sum" assigns it the number $8$.

Key idea: it is a function from outcomes to numbers, not a variable you solve for.
cards.searchQuery: random variable definition numerical outcome

cards.title: Name the three common interpretations of probability.
cards.body:
Classical, empirical (relative frequency) and subjective

- **Classical**: equally likely outcomes, $\frac{\text{favorable}}{\text{total}}$
- **Empirical**: long-run relative frequency of the event
- **Subjective**: a personal degree of belief

Example: "the chance of rain tomorrow is 30%" is usually empirical or subjective, since the outcomes aren't equally likely.
cards.searchQuery: classical empirical subjective probability interpretations

cards.title: One card is drawn from a standard 52-card deck. What is the probability that it is a face card (J, Q or K), as a fraction in lowest terms?
cards.body:
$\frac{3}{13} \approx 0.231$

A standard deck has $3 \times 4 = 12$ face cards (J, Q, K in four suits), so $P = \frac{12}{52} = \frac{3}{13}$.

Watch out: aces are not face cards in the usual definition.
cards.searchQuery: probability of drawing a face card

cards.title: Two fair dice are rolled. What is the probability that the sum is at least 9, as a fraction in lowest terms?
cards.body:
$\frac{5}{18} \approx 0.278$

List the favorable sums: 9 (4 ways), 10 (3 ways), 11 (2 ways), 12 (1 way), a total of $10$ of the $36$ outcomes. So $P = \frac{10}{36} = \frac{5}{18}$.

Tip: counting ordered pairs keeps all 36 outcomes equally likely.
cards.searchQuery: two dice sum at least 9 probability

cards.title: Two fair dice are rolled. What is the probability that at least one shows a 6, as a fraction?
cards.body:
$\frac{11}{36} \approx 0.306$

Use the complement: $1 - P(\text{no 6 on either die}) = 1 - \left(\frac{5}{6}\right)^2 = 1 - \frac{25}{36} = \frac{11}{36}$.

Watch out: $\frac{1}{6} + \frac{1}{6} = \frac{1}{3}$ double counts the outcome (6,6).
cards.searchQuery: two dice at least one six complement

cards.title: A fair coin is flipped 3 times. What is the probability of at least two heads, as a fraction?
cards.body:
$\frac{1}{2}$

Of the 8 equally likely sequences, exactly 3 have two heads (HHT, HTH, THH) and 1 has three heads (HHH), so $P = \frac{4}{8} = \frac{1}{2}$.

Tip: by symmetry, "at least two heads" and "at least two tails" together cover everything exactly once.
cards.searchQuery: three coin flips at least two heads

cards.title: What is the smallest group size for which the probability that two people share a birthday exceeds $\frac{1}{2}$?
cards.body:
23

With 23 people, $P(\text{shared birthday}) = 1 - \dfrac{365}{365} \cdot \dfrac{364}{365} \cdots \dfrac{343}{365} \approx 0.507$. With 22 people it is about $0.476$.

Why: the number of **pairs** grows like $\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$, so matches show up far sooner than intuition expects.
Tip: assume 365 equally likely birthdays and ignore leap years.
cards.searchQuery: birthday problem 23 people shared birthday

cards.title: Monty Hall: you pick one of 3 doors (1 car, 2 goats). The host, who knows where the car is, opens a different door showing a goat and offers a switch. What is the probability of winning if you switch?
cards.body:
$\frac{2}{3}$

Your first pick is right with probability $\frac{1}{3}$. The host always opens a goat door, so switching wins exactly when your first pick was wrong: $\frac{2}{3}$.

Watch out: the two remaining doors are not 50-50. The host's choice is not random, since he knows where the car is.
cards.searchQuery: Monty Hall problem probability of winning by switching

cards.title: Each of 3 days is rainy with probability $0.3$, independently. What is the probability that at least one day is rainy?
cards.body:
0.657

$P(\text{at least one}) = 1 - P(\text{no rain}) = 1 - 0.7^3 = 1 - 0.343 = 0.657$

Tip: "at least one" almost always means complement.
cards.searchQuery: probability of at least one rainy day independent

cards.title: $A$ and $B$ are independent, with $P(A) = 0.5$ and $P(B) = 0.3$. What is $P(A \cap B)$?
cards.body:
0.15

For independent events, $P(A \cap B) = P(A)\,P(B) = 0.5 \times 0.3 = 0.15$.

Watch out: this shortcut is valid only when the events are independent. Otherwise use $P(A)\,P(B \mid A)$.
cards.searchQuery: multiplication rule for independent events

cards.title: Events $A$ and $B$ are independent. Are $A$ and $B^c$ also independent? (Yes or no)
cards.body:
Yes

If $A$ and $B$ are independent, so are $A$ and $B^c$: $P(A \cap B^c) = P(A) - P(A)P(B) = P(A)\,(1 - P(B)) = P(A)\,P(B^c)$.

Key idea: knowing whether $B$ happened never changes the probability of $A$, in either direction.
cards.searchQuery: independent events complement also independent

cards.title: $A$ and $B$ are independent, with $P(A) = 0.3$ and $P(B) = 0.2$. What is $P(A \cup B)$?
cards.searchQuery: union of independent events probability

cards.title: A machine needs all 3 of its independent components to work, and each works with probability $0.9$. What is the probability that the machine works?
cards.body:
0.729

A series system works only if every component works: $0.9 \times 0.9 \times 0.9 = 0.729$.

Watch out: adding components in series makes the system less reliable, not more.
cards.searchQuery: series system reliability independent components

cards.title: Two independent backup pumps each work with probability $0.9$, and the system works if at least one does. What is the probability that the system works?
cards.body:
0.99

A parallel system fails only if both fail: $1 - (0.1)(0.1) = 1 - 0.01 = 0.99$.

Key idea: redundancy helps, and the complement makes it easy to compute.
cards.searchQuery: parallel system reliability backup component

cards.title: State the general multiplication rule for $P(A \cap B)$, valid even when $A$ and $B$ are dependent.
cards.body:
$P(A \cap B) = P(A)\,P(B \mid A)$

Multiply the probability of the first event by the probability of the second **given** the first. It is the conditional probability formula rearranged.

Tip: the order can be swapped: $P(A \cap B) = P(B)\,P(A \mid B)$.
cards.searchQuery: general multiplication rule P(A and B)

cards.title: $P(A \mid B) = 0.4$ and $P(B) = 0.5$. What is $P(A \cap B)$?
cards.body:
0.2

$P(A \cap B) = P(A \mid B)\,P(B) = 0.4 \times 0.5 = 0.2$

Watch out: don't add or average the two numbers. A joint probability is a conditional times a marginal.
cards.searchQuery: P(A and B) from conditional probability

cards.title: $P(A \mid B) = 0.3$. What is $P(A^c \mid B)$?
cards.body:
0.7

Given $B$, the outcomes are split into $A$ and $A^c$, so $P(A^c \mid B) = 1 - P(A \mid B) = 1 - 0.3 = 0.7$.

Watch out: $P(A^c \mid B) \ne 1 - P(A \mid B^c)$. The complement rule applies to the event, not the condition.
cards.searchQuery: complement of conditional probability

cards.title: Why is $P(\text{positive test} \mid \text{disease})$ usually not equal to $P(\text{disease} \mid \text{positive test})$?
cards.body:
Because $P(A \mid B)$ and $P(B \mid A)$ have different denominators and answer different questions.

Example: almost all professional basketball players are tall, but very few tall people are professional basketball players.

Tip: Bayes' theorem converts one into the other, but you need the base rate $P(A)$.
cards.searchQuery: confusing P(A given B) with P(B given A) transposed conditional

cards.title: Two cards are dealt in order without replacement from a standard 52-card deck. What is the probability that the first is an ace and the second is a king, as a fraction in lowest terms?
cards.body:
$\frac{4}{663} \approx 0.0060$

$P(\text{ace first}) = \frac{4}{52}$, then $P(\text{king} \mid \text{ace}) = \frac{4}{51}$, so $\frac{4}{52} \cdot \frac{4}{51} = \frac{16}{2652} = \frac{4}{663}$.

Tip: after the first draw only 51 cards remain, but all 4 kings are still there.
cards.searchQuery: probability ace then king without replacement

cards.title: A family has two children, each equally likely a boy or a girl, independently. Given that at least one is a boy, what is the probability that both are boys?
cards.body:
$\frac{1}{3}$

The equally likely families are BB, BG, GB, GG. "At least one boy" leaves BB, BG, GB, and only BB has two boys: $\frac{1}{3}$.

Watch out: the answer is not $\frac{1}{2}$. Compare the next card, where the older child is known to be a boy.
cards.searchQuery: two children at least one boy probability both boys

cards.title: A family has two children, each equally likely a boy or a girl, independently. Given that the older child is a boy, what is the probability that both are boys?
cards.body:
$\frac{1}{2}$

Knowing the older child is a boy leaves BB and BG, equally likely, so $P(\text{both boys}) = \frac{1}{2}$.

Why: the younger child is independent of the older one.
cards.searchQuery: two children older is a boy probability both boys

cards.title: A bag holds 5 red and 5 blue marbles. Two are drawn without replacement. What is the probability that both are red, as a fraction in lowest terms?
cards.body:
$\frac{2}{9} \approx 0.222$

$P(\text{both red}) = \frac{5}{10} \cdot \frac{4}{9} = \frac{20}{90} = \frac{2}{9}$

Watch out: with replacement it would be $\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{4}$.
cards.searchQuery: two red marbles drawn without replacement probability

cards.title: Two fair dice are rolled and the sum is 8. Given that, what is the probability that at least one die shows a 3, as a fraction?
cards.body:
$\frac{2}{5}$

Sum 8 has five equally likely outcomes: $(2,6), (3,5), (4,4), (5,3), (6,2)$. Two contain a 3, so $P = \frac{2}{5}$.

Tip: condition by shrinking the sample space to the outcomes that satisfy the given event.
cards.searchQuery: conditional probability dice sum 8 one die shows 3

cards.title: $A$ and $B$ are disjoint and $P(B) > 0$. What is $P(A \mid B)$?
cards.body:
0

If $A$ and $B$ are disjoint and $P(B) > 0$, then $P(A \mid B) = \dfrac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)} = \dfrac{0}{P(B)} = 0$.

Key idea: if $B$ happened, $A$ cannot have, so disjoint events are never independent (when both have positive probability).
cards.searchQuery: conditional probability of disjoint events zero

cards.title: Of 80 men, 20 are left-handed; of 120 women, 18 are. A left-handed person is chosen at random. What is the probability that the person is a man, as a fraction?
cards.body:
$\frac{10}{19} \approx 0.526$

Left-handed men: $20$. Left-handed women: $18$. So $P(\text{man} \mid \text{left-handed}) = \frac{20}{20 + 18} = \frac{20}{38} = \frac{10}{19}$.

Watch out: dividing by the 80 men would give $P(\text{left-handed} \mid \text{man}) = 0.25$, a different question.
cards.searchQuery: reverse conditioning two-way counts left-handed man

cards.title: What two properties must events $B_1, \dots, B_k$ have to be used in the law of total probability?
cards.body:
Mutually exclusive and exhaustive events

Events $B_1, \dots, B_k$ form a **partition** if they are disjoint and together cover the whole sample space, so exactly one of them occurs.

Key idea: the law of total probability needs a partition: $P(A) = \sum_i P(A \mid B_i)\,P(B_i)$.
cards.searchQuery: partition of sample space law of total probability mutually exclusive exhaustive

cards.title: Three suppliers provide 50%, 30% and 20% of a store's bulbs, with defect rates of 1%, 2% and 4%. What is the probability that a random bulb is defective?
cards.body:
0.019

$P(D) = (0.50)(0.01) + (0.30)(0.02) + (0.20)(0.04) = 0.005 + 0.006 + 0.008 = 0.019$

Watch out: the shares $0.5 + 0.3 + 0.2$ must add to 1. Check that the sources form a partition.
cards.searchQuery: law of total probability three suppliers defect rates

cards.title: Machine A makes 60% of a plant's parts (2% defective); Machine B makes 40% (5% defective). A randomly chosen part is defective. What is the probability that it came from Machine A?
cards.body:
0.375 (that is, $\frac{3}{8}$)

Machine A contributes $(0.02)(0.6) = 0.012$ of the $P(D) = 0.032$ total, so $P(A \mid D) = \dfrac{0.012}{0.032} = 0.375$.

Why: A makes 60% of the parts, but only 37.5% of the defective ones, because its defect rate is lower.
cards.searchQuery: Bayes theorem which machine made defective part

cards.title: Urn 1 holds 3 red and 1 blue ball; urn 2 holds 1 red and 3 blue. An urn is chosen at random and a ball drawn from it is red. What is the probability that it came from urn 1?
cards.body:
0.75

$P(\text{red}) = \frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{3}{4} + \frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{4} = \frac{1}{2}$, so $P(\text{urn 1} \mid \text{red}) = \dfrac{\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{3}{4}}{\frac{1}{2}} = \dfrac{3}{4}$.

Tip: with equal priors, the posterior is just the share of red among the two likelihoods: $\frac{0.75}{0.75 + 0.25}$.
cards.searchQuery: Bayes theorem two urns red ball drawn

cards.title: 40% of email is spam. The word "free" appears in 50% of spam and 10% of non-spam. What is $P(\text{spam} \mid \text{contains "free"})$, to three decimal places?
cards.body:
$\frac{10}{13} \approx 0.769$

$P(\text{spam} \mid \text{word}) = \dfrac{(0.5)(0.4)}{(0.5)(0.4) + (0.1)(0.6)} = \dfrac{0.20}{0.26} = \dfrac{10}{13}$

Tip: the numerator is one branch of the tree; the denominator adds all branches that end in the word.
cards.searchQuery: Bayes theorem spam filter word probability

cards.title: A test detects 90% of cases and falsely flags 5% of healthy people. If 10% of the people tested have the disease, what is $P(\text{disease} \mid \text{positive})$, to three decimal places?
cards.body:
$\frac{2}{3} \approx 0.667$

$P(D \mid +) = \dfrac{(0.90)(0.10)}{(0.90)(0.10) + (0.05)(0.90)} = \dfrac{0.09}{0.135} = \dfrac{2}{3}$

Key idea: the same test is far more trustworthy when the condition is common. With a 1% prevalence the answer was only about 0.154.
cards.searchQuery: Bayes theorem effect of prevalence positive predictive value

cards.title: What is base rate neglect?
cards.body:
Ignoring the **base rate** (prior probability), so that a test's accuracy is mistaken for the chance that a positive is a true positive.

When a condition is rare, even a small false-positive rate produces many more false alarms than true cases.

Tip: picture 1,000 people instead of probabilities. Count true positives and false positives, then compare them.
cards.searchQuery: base rate neglect fallacy rare disease

cards.title: Define the sensitivity and the specificity of a diagnostic test as conditional probabilities.
cards.body:
**Sensitivity** is $P(+ \mid \text{condition})$; **specificity** is $P(- \mid \text{no condition})$.

Sensitivity is the true positive rate; specificity is the true negative rate.

Watch out: the false-positive rate is $1 - \text{specificity}$, not $1 - \text{sensitivity}$.
cards.searchQuery: sensitivity and specificity definitions test

cards.title: $P(A) = 0.3$, $P(B) = 0.5$ and $P(A \mid B) = 0.2$. What is $P(B \mid A)$, as a fraction?
cards.body:
$\frac{1}{3} \approx 0.333$

$P(B \mid A) = \dfrac{P(A \mid B)\,P(B)}{P(A)} = \dfrac{0.2 \times 0.5}{0.3} = \dfrac{0.1}{0.3} = \dfrac{1}{3}$

Tip: the numerator is the joint probability $P(A \cap B) = 0.1$.
cards.searchQuery: Bayes theorem reverse conditional numbers P(B given A)

cards.title: In the odds form of Bayes' rule, what do you multiply the prior odds by to get the posterior odds?
cards.body:
Posterior odds = prior odds $\times$ likelihood ratio

$\dfrac{P(H \mid E)}{P(H^c \mid E)} = \dfrac{P(H)}{P(H^c)} \times \dfrac{P(E \mid H)}{P(E \mid H^c)}$

Example: 1% prevalence (odds $\frac{1}{99}$), and a positive result with likelihood ratio $\frac{0.90}{0.05} = 18$: posterior odds $\frac{18}{99}$, so $P \approx 0.154$.
cards.searchQuery: Bayes rule odds form posterior odds prior odds likelihood ratio

cards.title: An outfit is 1 of 5 shirts, 1 of 4 pairs of pants and 1 of 2 pairs of shoes. How many different outfits are there?
cards.body:
40

Choices made one after another multiply: $5 \times 4 \times 2 = 40$.

Watch out: use addition only when the choices are alternatives (either/or), not steps in a sequence.
cards.searchQuery: fundamental counting principle multiplication principle outfits

cards.title: In how many different orders can 5 people stand in a line?
cards.body:
120

There are $5$ choices for the first spot, $4$ for the next, and so on: $5! = 5 \cdot 4 \cdot 3 \cdot 2 \cdot 1 = 120$.

Tip: $n$ distinct objects can be ordered in $n!$ ways, and $0! = 1$.
cards.searchQuery: arrange 5 people in a row factorial

cards.title: Eight runners compete. In how many ways can the gold, silver and bronze medals be awarded (no ties)?
cards.body:
336

Order matters (gold, silver, bronze are different), so $P(8, 3) = \dfrac{8!}{5!} = 8 \cdot 7 \cdot 6 = 336$.

Watch out: $\binom{8}{3} = 56$ counts only the groups of three, ignoring who gets which medal.
cards.searchQuery: permutations gold silver bronze 8 runners

cards.title: A lottery draws 6 numbers from 1 to 49, order not mattering. How many different draws are possible?
cards.body:
13,983,816

Order doesn't matter, so $\binom{49}{6} = \dfrac{49 \cdot 48 \cdot 47 \cdot 46 \cdot 45 \cdot 44}{6!} = 13{,}983{,}816$.

Tip: the chance of matching all six is one in about 14 million.
cards.searchQuery: lottery odds combination 6 of 49

cards.title: How many different 5-card hands can be dealt from a standard 52-card deck?
cards.body:
2,598,960

A hand is an unordered set of 5 cards: $\binom{52}{5} = \dfrac{52 \cdot 51 \cdot 50 \cdot 49 \cdot 48}{5!} = 2{,}598{,}960$.

Key idea: this is the denominator for every five-card hand probability.
cards.searchQuery: number of five-card poker hands combination

cards.title: How many distinct arrangements are there of the letters in the word BOOK?
cards.body:
12

Divide by the repeats: $\dfrac{4!}{2!} = \dfrac{24}{2} = 12$ distinct arrangements of B, O, O, K.

Why: swapping the two O's doesn't create a new word, so each arrangement was counted $2!$ times.
cards.searchQuery: arrangements of letters with repeats BOOK

cards.title: What is $\binom{12}{10}$?
cards.body:
66

Symmetry: $\binom{12}{10} = \binom{12}{2} = \dfrac{12 \cdot 11}{2} = 66$.

Why: choosing the 10 people to include is the same as choosing the 2 to leave out.
cards.searchQuery: binomial coefficient symmetry C(n,r) = C(n,n-r)

cards.title: In how many distinct ways can 5 people sit around a circular table if rotations count as the same seating?
cards.body:
24

Fix one person's seat to remove rotations; the other 4 can be arranged in $4! = 24$ ways.

Key idea: for $n$ people around a circle, there are $(n-1)!$ seatings when only the relative order counts.
cards.searchQuery: seating people around a circular table arrangements

cards.title: A code is 3 letters (A to Z) followed by 2 digits (0 to 9), and repeats are allowed. How many codes are possible?
cards.body:
1,757,600

Each of the 3 letter slots has 26 choices and each of the 2 digit slots has 10: $26^3 \cdot 10^2 = 17{,}576 \times 100 = 1{,}757{,}600$.

Watch out: repeats are allowed here, so use powers rather than $P(26, 3)$.
cards.searchQuery: password count letters then digits multiplication principle

cards.title: A committee of 5 is chosen from 6 men and 5 women, with exactly 3 men and 2 women. How many committees are possible?
cards.body:
200

Choose the men and the women separately, then multiply: $\binom{6}{3}\binom{5}{2} = 20 \times 10 = 200$.

Tip: "and" between independent selections means multiply; don't use $\binom{11}{5}$, which ignores the required mix.
cards.searchQuery: committee with 3 men and 2 women combinations

cards.title: A 5-card hand is dealt from a standard deck. What is the probability that it contains exactly 2 aces? Round to 4 decimal places.
cards.body:
0.0399

$P = \dfrac{\binom{4}{2}\binom{48}{3}}{\binom{52}{5}} = \dfrac{6 \times 17{,}296}{2{,}598{,}960} = \dfrac{103{,}776}{2{,}598{,}960} \approx 0.0399$

Tip: count favorable hands as (ways to pick the aces) times (ways to fill the rest with non-aces).
cards.searchQuery: probability exactly two aces in a five-card hand counting

cards.title: What is the formula for the expected value $E(X)$ of a discrete random variable $X$?
cards.body:
$E(X) = \sum x\,P(X = x)$

Multiply each possible value by its probability and add. It is the long-run average of $X$, not necessarily a value $X$ can take.

Example: a fair die has $E(X) = \frac{1 + 2 + \cdots + 6}{6} = 3.5$.
cards.searchQuery: expected value of discrete random variable formula

cards.title: $X$ takes the values $1$, $2$ and $3$ with probabilities $0.5$, $0.3$ and $0.2$. What is $E(X)$?
cards.body:
1.7

$E(X) = 1(0.5) + 2(0.3) + 3(0.2) = 0.5 + 0.6 + 0.6 = 1.7$

Watch out: the plain average of $1, 2, 3$ is $2$, which ignores the unequal probabilities.
cards.searchQuery: expected value from probability table

cards.title: A random variable takes four values with probabilities $0.2$, $0.3$, $c$ and $0.1$. What is $c$?
cards.body:
0.4

Probabilities must sum to $1$: $0.2 + 0.3 + c + 0.1 = 1$, so $c = 0.4$.

Tip: always check this first. It also catches any value outside $[0, 1]$.
cards.searchQuery: missing probability in distribution sum to 1

cards.title: What is the expected value of one roll of a fair six-sided die?
cards.body:
3.5

$E(X) = \frac{1}{6}(1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6) = \frac{21}{6} = 3.5$

Watch out: $3.5$ is not a possible roll. The expected value is a long-run average.
cards.searchQuery: expected value of a fair die roll

cards.title: $E(X) = 5$. What is $E(2X + 3)$?
cards.body:
13

$E(aX + b) = aE(X) + b$, so $E(2X + 3) = 2(5) + 3 = 13$.

Key idea: expectation is linear, and this holds for any distribution of $X$.
cards.searchQuery: expected value of aX + b linearity

cards.title: $E(X) = 10$ and $E(Y) = 4$. What is $E(X - Y)$?
cards.body:
6

$E(X - Y) = E(X) - E(Y) = 10 - 4 = 6$

Tip: unlike variances, means subtract exactly, and independence isn't needed.
cards.searchQuery: expected value of difference E(X - Y)

cards.title: Two fair dice are rolled. What is the expected value of their sum?
cards.body:
7

By linearity, $E(X_1 + X_2) = E(X_1) + E(X_2) = 3.5 + 3.5 = 7$.

Key idea: linearity of expectation needs **no independence**. It works even when the variables depend on each other.
cards.searchQuery: expected sum of two dice linearity of expectation

cards.title: A raffle ticket costs 2 dollars and wins a 1000-dollar prize with probability $\frac{1}{1000}$ (otherwise nothing). What is the expected net gain per ticket, in dollars?
cards.body:
$-1$ dollar per ticket

Expected prize: $1000 \times \frac{1}{1000} = 1$ dollar. Net: $1 - 2 = -1$ dollar.

Watch out: subtract the ticket price. The expected prize alone is a gain of 1 dollar; the expected net result is a loss of 1 dollar.
cards.searchQuery: expected net winnings lottery ticket

cards.title: A game costs 5 dollars to play and pays 20 dollars with probability $\frac{1}{4}$ (otherwise nothing). Is it a fair game, meaning an expected net gain of 0? (Yes or no)
cards.body:
Yes

$E(\text{net}) = 20\left(\frac{1}{4}\right) + 0\left(\frac{3}{4}\right) - 5 = 5 - 5 = 0$, so it is a **fair game**.

Tip: a game is fair when the expected net gain is $0$ for the player.
cards.searchQuery: fair game expected value zero

cards.title: In American roulette, 18 of 38 equally likely slots are red. A 1-dollar bet on red wins 1 dollar if red comes up, else loses it. What is the expected net gain, in dollars? Round to 4 decimal places.
cards.body:
$-\frac{1}{19} \approx -0.0526$

$E = (+1)\frac{18}{38} + (-1)\frac{20}{38} = -\frac{2}{38} = -\frac{1}{19}$ per 1-dollar bet.

Key idea: a small negative expected value is the house edge. It guarantees a loss in the long run.
cards.searchQuery: roulette expected value bet on red

cards.title: Write two equivalent formulas for the variance of a random variable $X$ with mean $\mu$.
cards.body:
$\operatorname{Var}(X) = E\big[(X - \mu)^2\big] = E(X^2) - \mu^2$

The variance is the average squared distance from the mean $\mu = E(X)$; the second form is usually easier to compute.

Watch out: $E(X^2) \ne [E(X)]^2$ unless $X$ is constant.
cards.searchQuery: variance of a random variable definition shortcut

cards.title: What is the variance of one roll of a fair six-sided die? Round to 2 decimal places.
cards.searchQuery: variance of one roll of a fair die

cards.title: $\operatorname{Var}(X) = 4$. What is $\operatorname{Var}(3X + 2)$?
cards.body:
36

$\operatorname{Var}(aX + b) = a^2 \operatorname{Var}(X) = 3^2(4) = 36$

Watch out: the constant $b$ doesn't affect the variance, and $a$ is **squared** (so the SD scales by $|a| = 3$).
cards.searchQuery: variance of aX + b scaling squares

cards.title: $X_1, X_2, X_3$ are independent, each with variance $4$. What is $\operatorname{Var}(X_1 + X_2 + X_3)$?
cards.body:
12

For independent variables, variances add: $\operatorname{Var}(X_1 + X_2 + X_3) = 4 + 4 + 4 = 12$.

Watch out: this is not $\operatorname{Var}(3X) = 9 \cdot 4 = 36$, which would treat the three as the same variable.
cards.searchQuery: variance of sum of independent identically distributed variables

cards.title: $X$ and $Y$ are independent with the same variance $\sigma^2$. How do $\operatorname{Var}(2X)$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X + Y)$ compare?
cards.body:
$\operatorname{Var}(2X) = 4\sigma^2$, but $\operatorname{Var}(X + Y) = 2\sigma^2$.

Doubling one variable stretches it fully ($b^2 = 4$). Adding an independent copy lets the two partly cancel, so the variances simply add.

Example: two separate dice have a smaller relative spread in their sum than one die doubled.
cards.searchQuery: variance 2X versus X plus independent copy

cards.title: For possibly dependent $X$ and $Y$, what is $\operatorname{Var}(X + Y)$?
cards.body:
$\operatorname{Var}(X + Y) = \operatorname{Var}(X) + \operatorname{Var}(Y) + 2\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y)$

The covariance term vanishes when $X$ and $Y$ are independent (or just uncorrelated).

Tip: positive covariance makes the sum more variable; negative covariance makes it less variable (as in hedging).
cards.searchQuery: variance of sum with covariance correlated variables

cards.title: $X$ equals $0$ or $10$, each with probability $0.5$. What is the standard deviation of $X$?
cards.body:
5

$\mu = 0(0.5) + 10(0.5) = 5$. Each value is $5$ away from the mean, so $\operatorname{Var}(X) = 25$ and $\sigma = \sqrt{25} = 5$.

Tip: here $\sigma$ equals the typical distance from the mean exactly, because both deviations are the same size.
cards.searchQuery: standard deviation from probability distribution 0 or 10

cards.title: $I_A$ equals $1$ if event $A$ occurs and $0$ otherwise. What is $E(I_A)$?
cards.body:
$P(A)$

For $I_A = 1$ if $A$ occurs and $0$ otherwise, $E(I_A) = 1 \cdot P(A) + 0 \cdot P(A^c) = P(A)$.

Key idea: counting events with indicators turns expected counts into sums of probabilities, via linearity.
cards.searchQuery: expected value of indicator variable equals probability
